video_title: Is IMAX a Screaming Buy? | LFTC
gist: IMAX CEO Rich Gelfond argues IMAX has become a structural gatekeeper in Hollywood — an IMAX slot is now part of the studio green-light process and filmmakers pitch IMAX before they have a distributor — while the hosts press him on why a brand they rate alongside Disney and Nike still carries only a ~$3B market cap. Gelfond details the untapped monetization levers (merchandise, film prints, mispriced IMAX tickets at AMC, a China automotive AV licensing deal) and the 2027-28 slate backlog that gives IMAX unusual forward visibility.

themes.theme: IMAX inside the studio green-light process

insights.claim: IMAX has moved upstream from a distribution add-on to part of the green-light decision itself: at most major studios an IMAX release slot is negotiated when a film is approved, alongside studio marketing commitments (Paramount and Tom Cruise both committed spend and promotion for Mission: Impossible 8 right after MI7 finished its run).
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: If IMAX is embedded at green-light, its revenue is contracted years ahead and its negotiating leverage on marketing and date selection rises — a structurally better position than a per-film licensor.
insights.quote: So the business like you know we're part of the green light process now and I would say at most of the major studios an IMAX release is part of the green light.

insights.claim: IMAX turned down Avengers: Doomsday at Christmas to honor an earlier commitment to Denis Villeneuve's Dune 3, which was shot in part on IMAX cameras and will get the same number of film prints as The Odyssey.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: Christmas 2026 IMAX box office rides on Dune 3 rather than a Marvel tentpole — a concentrated, checkable catalyst — and the refusal signals IMAX will trade near-term revenue for filmmaker loyalty that locks in future slots.
insights.quote: we love you guys and we love to do your movie but we have a commitment and that's the currency that we're made of

insights.claim: Filmmakers now approach IMAX directly before a distributor is attached — Jerry Bruckheimer and Joseph Kosinski locked an IMAX date for F1 more than a year out and only then went to Warner Bros.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: Being the first call rather than the last gives IMAX first pick of dates and screens, and shows the moat is talent relationships, not just hardware — hard for a repackaged large-format competitor to replicate.

themes.theme: The Odyssey: box office proof points and indexing

insights.claim: Through 24 days The Odyssey did roughly $461 million domestic versus $264 million for Oppenheimer over the same window, a comparison the hosts attribute largely to IMAX pre-sales and Nolan shooting the entire film on IMAX cameras.
insights.speaker: host (Michael)
insights.so_what: A ~75% uplift over the prior Nolan benchmark is the cleanest available evidence that IMAX-native production materially expands a film's total gross, which is the argument for higher IMAX take rates.

insights.claim: The Odyssey will be near $300 million of IMAX box office with another $40 million already in pre-sales and a run through September, so roughly $340 million is effectively booked before another ticket is sold.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: A single title contributing well over $300M of IMAX gross reframes the per-film ceiling and directly supports full-year guidance; the $40M pre-sale backlog is a near-riskless revenue line.

insights.claim: IMAX's own film team modeled an 'ultimate' of $190 million for The Odyssey while Gelfond argued for over $300 million — and he says even his own forecast was too low, implying internal forecasting systematically understates IMAX-native event films.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: If IMAX's internal ultimates run low on event titles, sell-side models anchored to company guidance are likely conservative on the biggest releases — an upside-surprise pattern to watch on Dune 3.
insights.quote: at IMAX, we had an ultimate of 190 for the movie. That's what my film team thought it would do. And I said it would do over 300.

insights.claim: IMAX indexed around 26% of The Odyssey's box office and has exceeded 30% on some titles, but Gelfond frames indexing as a function of how many screens a film opens on and what regular theaters are doing rather than a number to maximize.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: Indexing is the key per-film revenue metric; understanding it caps out near 26-30% on wide releases sets a realistic ceiling for modeling IMAX's share of any single blockbuster.

insights.claim: Gelfond says the required input for an IMAX title's success is the director leaning in during pre-production, not the technology — citing Nolan's 15-item demand list (including the sound-dampening 'blimp' and global spare-parts depots), Ryan Coogler's aspect-ratio explainer for Sinners, and Villeneuve on Dune 3.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: A usable screen for which upcoming IMAX titles will overperform: check whether the director publicly frames the film as IMAX-native, rather than counting screens.
insights.quote: it's not just the technology and you need the filmmaker to say this is the way I made it and this is what the way they're thinking about IMAX as they're like in pre-production for the film

themes.theme: Untapped monetization: merch, ticket pricing, film prints

insights.claim: IMAX started merchandising only this year and demand overwhelmed a deliberately conservative rollout: 2,500 IMAX-camera popcorn buckets sold in two hours, another 2,500 in under an hour, 2,500 in China in 60 seconds, and 20,000 Odyssey film strips in 90 minutes.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: A brand-monetization line starting from near zero with instant sell-throughs is a high-margin, non-box-office revenue stream not yet in most models — watch for a scaled merch program around Dune 3.
insights.quote: So, we put 2500 on sale and they sold in 2 hours.

insights.claim: IMAX does not set ticket prices and is being underpriced by its largest exhibitor: AMC in New York charges the same price for an IMAX film ticket as a regular ticket and sells it at half price on Wednesdays (~$14), while Brendan Theaters in Las Vegas charges $50 for IMAX film and sells out.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: A ~3.5x price gap between exhibitors on identical product is pure captured-value upside if exhibitors adopt dynamic or premium pricing — an underappreciated option on IMAX's per-screen economics.
insights.quote: AMC here in New York is charging the same price for an IMAX film ticket as they are for a regular ticket.

insights.claim: Film (versus digital) IMAX releases carry higher ticket prices, higher utilization and higher indexing, but each 70mm print costs about $50,000 and the projectors — built roughly 50 years ago and scavenged rather than manufactured — cost more, so film can only be deployed in very high-traffic locations.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: Explains why IMAX cannot simply expand its highest-margin format on demand; print and projector economics, not demand, are the binding constraint on the premium tier.
insights.quote: So, one print at one theater, so think of the one that shows at 68th Street here in Manhattan, cost $50,000.

insights.claim: The 70mm film footprint has grown from 30 theaters at Oppenheimer to 41 globally (around 25 in the US), roughly four IMAX film titles are slated for next year, and Gelfond says an unproven new idea could add about 10 more — with the LA Live conversion done January 1 doing $800,000 in its first six months.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: A ~37% increase in the highest-indexing screen base since Oppenheimer, plus a possible further 25% step-up, is a quantifiable driver of per-title IMAX gross on the 2027 slate.

insights.claim: IMAX operates 800 theaters in China and released Ne Zha there, a film Gelfond notes the US audience has not heard of that grossed about $1.2 billion — evidence IMAX's economics are not solely a bet on Hollywood output.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: China local-language blockbusters can offset a weak Hollywood slate year, diversifying the single biggest perceived risk in the IMAX story.

insights.claim: IMAX's local-language and international film business has compounded at a 24% CAGR from 2019 to 2025, spanning anime released worldwide rather than only in Japan and a big Indian title being opened globally next — titles no theater chain is otherwise playing.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: A 24% CAGR segment inside a company priced on Hollywood tentpole risk is the most direct rebuttal to the 'lumpy slate' bear case — and it is largely uncontested white space.

insights.claim: IMAX programmed 120 pieces of content last year including concerts (a live Stop Making Sense event with David Byrne from Toronto), NBA Finals in China, NHL tests in Europe, an HBO series and an Interstellar re-release that did over $5 million — but marketing cost, not availability, limits how many catalog titles can be re-released, so only iconic titles work.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: Sets the realistic size of the alternative-content filler business: it smooths box-office gaps only for titles that can carry a standalone marketing spend, so don't model unlimited catalog monetization.

themes.theme: Forward visibility: backlog, guidance and the 2027-28 slate

insights.claim: Gelfond argues IMAX has more forward visibility than almost any business because it publicly guides on a theater installation backlog and has films contractually committed into 2028 and some into 2029, including all four Sam Mendes Beatles films for Sony in 2028 and a Bond title.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: Directly attacks the 'unpredictable 2027-28' discount the hosts say Wall Street applies; the theater backlog and film commitments are disclosed and checkable against that discount.
insights.quote: I I would argue that we have more visibility into the future than almost any other business cuz if you're a car company, you have zero sales on opening day.

insights.claim: The 2027 IMAX slate discussed includes The Legend of Zelda (Nintendo IP, whose director cold-called Gelfond a year ahead insisting on IMAX), a new Ryan Gosling Star Wars film, Frozen 3, Minecraft, Shrek 5, The Mummy and Great Beyond, with the Avengers sequel at Christmas the following year — and Gelfond notes few movies were made in 2026 while many were made for 2027.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: A dense, mostly pre-signed 2027 slate against a thin 2026 production year argues against the feared post-Odyssey air pocket in 2027 revenue.
insights.quote: this year a lot of movies weren't made. Next year a lot of movies were made. So I think we're going to do very well.

insights.claim: IMAX guided to $1.2 billion in global box office last year and came in around $1.3 billion; this year it guided to $1.4 billion and Gelfond says the company is roughly $300 million away with seven months of results behind it.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: A guide-and-beat track record plus a specific run-rate against the current target gives a concrete checkpoint for whether 2026 guidance is again conservative.

themes.theme: Valuation gap, M&A posture and industry structure

insights.claim: The hosts argue IMAX's brand-to-market-cap ratio is one of the most lopsided in the stock market — the stock was pitched at $17 on May 14, 2024 at roughly a $1 billion cap and now sits near $3 billion — and that Wall Street's remaining discount reflects dislike of uncertainty about which films come out in 2027 and 2028 rather than the current business.
insights.speaker: host (Michael)
insights.so_what: Frames the bull case precisely: the re-rating from ~$1B to ~$3B has happened, so incremental upside depends on closing the slate-uncertainty discount, which the backlog disclosures can do.
insights.quote: the amount of influence and brand recognition that you have compared to your market cap was a joke. I thought it was very lopsided at a billion dollars.

insights.claim: NRG brand studies place IMAX's brand on the level of Disney and Nike, and Gelfond concedes the company gets very little recognition of that brand value in relative monetization — which is the explicit rationale for merchandising, licensing and the automotive AV deal.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: Management is openly naming the brand-monetization gap as the value-creation lever, so new non-theatrical revenue lines are the metric to track for a re-rating.
insights.quote: Well, we've done brand studies with NRG and our brand is on a level of Disney and Nike and people like that.

insights.claim: Gelfond contrasts IMAX's asset-light retrofit model with Sphere, which he says cost close to $3 billion for one venue — he says he would not own the stock, does not buy on narrative the way he passed on SpaceX, and invests on earnings and cash flow, while conceding Sphere's move to licensing is a better model than building each venue.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: The comparison the hosts raise — a globally scaled brand that can convert existing theaters versus a $3B single-venue capex model — is the core relative-value argument for IMAX over premium-venue peers.
insights.quote: I personally, I wouldn't own that stock. I didn't buy SpaceX. I don't put my finger in the air and say, "Hey, this is worth $2 trillion." Not the way I invest. I like looking at earnings and cash flow.

insights.claim: On takeover speculation Gelfond says people have been kicking the tires over a very long period, IMAX is not actively seeking a buyer, and the best thing that happened to the company was not selling 10 years ago — but he will talk at a blowaway price.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: There is no live process, so IMAX should not be owned for a near-term takeout; management's stated bar is a premium price, which caps M&A optionality as a thesis leg.
insights.quote: the best thing that's happened to this company is that it didn't sell 10 years ago because we've said we have so much promise in it and we run it to maximize shareholder value

insights.claim: Gelfond refuses to call the Paramount-Warner situation good or bad, arguing prognosticators have almost always been wrong about the movie business, and notes the offsetting positives: streamers as a large new content source, David Ellison's promise of 30 movies a year and a newly announced 45-day theatrical window.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: A 45-day window plus 30 films a year from a consolidated studio is a volume tailwind for exhibition that partly offsets losing Warner Bros as an independent buyer of content.
insights.quote: You know, the prognosticators, if I could say one thing about them, they've almost always been wrong about the future of the movie business.

insights.claim: Streaming platforms have become among IMAX's best content partners — Apple's F1 did $100 million in IMAX and $600 million overall as Apple's biggest release, Amazon's Hail Mary also did $100 million in IMAX, and Netflix is giving David Fincher's Cliff Booth (written by Tarantino, starring Brad Pitt) an exclusive IMAX theatrical run between Thanksgiving and Christmas before streaming.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: Streamers using IMAX exclusivity to eventize launches converts the historic streaming threat into a new demand pool; the Netflix Cliff Booth exclusive is the near-term test case.

insights.claim: Disney's Infinity Vision is a marketing bundle of existing branded screens rather than newly built large-format theaters, launched because Disney could not get IMAX screens for Avengers, and Gelfond says he is not losing sleep over it.
insights.speaker: Rich Gelfond, IMAX CEO
insights.so_what: The most obvious competitive threat to the IMAX moat is, per the CEO, repackaged existing capacity — worth watching whether consumers price Infinity Vision tickets like IMAX or like a regular screen.
insights.quote: But Infinity Vision is a marketing technique that's they're not building new theaters. They're taking existing theaters with an X in them and they're bundling them and they're calling it Infinity Vision.
